evidence.claim: Horse farms line the road between Midway and Versailles.
evidence.quote: Beautifully landscaped farms such as Fawn Leap, Shadowlawn, Adena Springs, Stonewall, and Land’s End are along the route between Parrish Avenue in Midway and the junction of US 60 in Versailles as you travel US Highway 62.

evidence.claim: The Midway-Versailles Road follows US 62 for 6.3 miles between Parrish Avenue in Midway and US 60 in Versailles.
evidence.quote: Beginning at Parrish Avenue in Midway via US 62 to the junction with US 60 in Versailles, a distance of 6.3 miles.

evidence.claim: Designated a state byway in 1995, it runs through horse-farm country.
evidence.quote: Designation State Byway (1995)

evidence.claim: The National Scenic Byway Foundation draws attention to the landscaped farms along the route, including Fawn Leap, Shadowlawn and Stonewall.
evidence.quote: Beautifully landscaped farms such as Fawn Leap, Shadowlawn, Adena Springs, Stonewall, and Land’s End are along the route

evidence.claim: Midway’s origins lie in a railroad’s purchase of farmland.
evidence.quote: The railroad then used the land to establish Kentucky's first railroad town

evidence.claim: In 1835, the Lexington and Ohio Railroad bought John Francisco’s farm and laid out Kentucky’s first railroad town.
evidence.quote: On January 31, 1835, the local farmer John Francisco sold his 216.375-acre (87.564 ha) farm to the Lexington and Ohio Railroad

evidence.claim: It called the settlement Middleway for its position between Lexington and Frankfort and named major streets for railroad officials.
evidence.quote: naming it Middleway for its location relative to Lexington and Frankfort, Kentucky. (The town is also equidistant between Versailles and Georgetown.) The major streets of Midway were named in honor of the railroad's original officials.

evidence.claim: The name became Midway in 1837.
evidence.quote: It was renamed Midway in 1837.

evidence.claim: laid out Kentucky’s first railroad town.
evidence.quote: The railroad then used the land to establish Kentucky's first railroad town

evidence.claim: Begin at Parrish Avenue and follow US 62 toward Versailles through the farms.
evidence.quote: along the route between Parrish Avenue in Midway and the junction of US 60 in Versailles as you travel US Highway 62.

evidence.claim: Versailles is the Woodford County seat, founded in 1792 on land owned by a child, Hezekiah Briscoe.
evidence.quote: Versailles was founded on June 23, 1792, on 80 acres (32 hectares) of land owned by Hezekiah Briscoe, who was, at the time, only a child.

evidence.claim: The designated drive ends at US 60; a separate excursion to the Bluegrass Railroad and Museum outside Versailles continues the area’s railway story.
evidence.quote: In 1988 the museum moved to its present location on Hwy 62 outside Versailles, Kentucky.

evidence.claim: Versailles is the Woodford County seat
evidence.quote: It is the county seat of Woodford County.

evidence.claim: The designated drive ends at US 60
evidence.quote: via US 62 to the junction with US 60 in Versailles

evidence.claim: Midway’s major streets were named for the officials of the railroad that established the town.
evidence.quote: The major streets of Midway were named in honor of the railroad's original officials.

evidence.claim: One street acquired a less formal name after a distillery warehouse fire on August 4, 1908.
evidence.quote: A large Distillery warehouse fire occurred on August 4, 1908

evidence.claim: More than 47,000 barrels of bourbon were destroyed, and Lee’s Branch burned for over a mile.
evidence.quote: over 47,000 barrels of bourbon where destroyed. The Lee's Branch was on fire for over one mile

evidence.claim: Residents who dipped tin cups into the stream for bourbon and water were scorched.
evidence.quote: several Midway residents were scorched dipping tin cups into the Lee's Branch for Bourbon and Water.

evidence.claim: Martin Street, beside the branch, became known as Tin Cup Alley.
evidence.quote: Martin Street next to the Lee's Branch was nicknamed “Tin Cup Alley”.

evidence.claim: Much of downtown belongs to the Midway Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: Midway Historic District comprises much of downtown Midway, and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: Versailles has a French name with a Kentucky pronunciation: vər-SAYLZ.
evidence.quote: The city's name is pronounced  vər-SAYLZ, an anglicization different from the French pronunciation

evidence.claim: The town was founded on June 23, 1792, on 80 acres belonging to Hezekiah Briscoe, then a child.
evidence.quote: Versailles was founded on June 23, 1792, on 80 acres (32 hectares) of land owned by Hezekiah Briscoe, who was, at the time, only a child.

evidence.claim: His guardian, Marquis Calmes, chose the name to honor Lafayette, a family friend and Revolutionary War figure.
evidence.quote: His guardian, Marquis Calmes, named the town after Versailles, France, in honor of General Lafayette, a family friend and hero of the American Revolution.

evidence.claim: Formal incorporation followed in 1837.
evidence.quote: the city was officially incorporated on February 13, 1837.

evidence.claim: The county seat lies in the Inner Bluegrass, where horse breeding and training include thoroughbreds, standardbreds and saddlebreds.
evidence.quote: In the Inner Bluegrass Region, the area is a center for horse breeding and training, and for thoroughbred and standardbred racehorses and saddlebred pleasure horses.

evidence.claim: A threatened rail line became the backbone of the Bluegrass Railroad and Museum outside Versailles.
evidence.quote: the portion of the line between the Kentucky River and Versailles was slated for abandonment, and subsequently sold to the museum.

evidence.claim: Members of a model railroad club founded the museum in 1976 and began collecting equipment from local railroads.
evidence.quote: The museum was founded in 1976 by some members of the Bluegrass Railroad Club, a model railroad group. It began to acquire equipment from local railroads

evidence.claim: The museum acquired five and a half miles of track toward the Kentucky River in 1987–1988.
evidence.quote: In 1987–1988 five and a half miles of railroad line from Versailles, Kentucky to the Kentucky River

evidence.claim: That line had been built by the Louisville Southern Railroad in the 1880s.
evidence.quote: The rail line was originally built by the Louisville Southern Railroad in the 1880s.

evidence.claim: After a 2006 fire, a partially burned house was remodeled as the station and museum.
evidence.quote: After a fire in 2006, a partially burned house was remodeled into a Station and Museum.

evidence.claim: The distillery had operated beside Lee’s Branch at Gratz and Dudley streets.
evidence.quote: The Distillery was located at the corner of Gratz Street and Dudley Street, nestled in the bend of the Lee's Branch

evidence.claim: The museum moved to its present site in 1988, after storing its collection at several locations in and near Lexington.
evidence.quote: The equipment was moved to a siding at Eastern State Hospital in Lexington, Kentucky, then to the Bluegrass Army Depot grounds in Avon, Kentucky. In 1988 the museum moved to its present location
